name: Lapse Capital: a land bank built on expired survey data

votes.strongest_objection: The ceiling is too low and the buyers are the wrong kind of buyer. The people who pay at this rung are cash-poor juniors (Purecore-type optionees). They pay small option cash and shares, and the work commitments they sign are spent on drilling, not paid to the vendor. Their spending follows equity financing windows: per S&P, exploration budgets fell for a third straight year in 2025 and grassroots spend hit a record-low share. So recurring revenue is capped at roughly US$5-30M/yr (estimate) even with 20-40 live options. The only venture-scale upside is a retained 1-3% NSR on a Tier-1 discovery. That is a lottery ticket that pays out 5-10+ years later, and the optionee and the eventual major capture most of the value. The closest peers prove the ceiling. Skyharbour already runs this exact vend-and-retain model on 15 Athabasca partner projects and is a small-cap. EMX, Eagle Plains and CanAlaska are worth tens to hundreds of millions, not billions (estimate). Lapsed ground is visible on MARS to every generator and major, and it carries adverse selection: the owner dropped it after judging the conductors not worth drilling. So the asset the company re-stakes is, on average, worth less than the archive's re-fly cost implies. ML is not what makes the work possible (conventional re-inversion by CGI, Mira and Condor already does it). It is structurally Terranox's own loop applied to a different data layer.
votes.evidence: Verified this run: Skyharbour's prospect-generator page lists 15 partner projects (Preston, Russell Lake, East Preston, Hook Lake, Falcon, South Falcon East, Mann Lake, South Dufferin, Bolt, Highway, Genie, Usam, Shoe and CBX, 914W, Yurchison). Yurchison was optioned to Purecore in 2026, so the identical model is already run at scale by an incumbent whose market value stays small-cap (estimate; not re-verified). Carried from prior research, not re-fetched: S&P World Exploration Trends 2026 reports budgets down for a third year in 2025 and record-low grassroots share, which hits junior optionee demand directly. Unverified/estimates: Paladin-Fission deal at about C$1.1B; a 2% NSR on it worth roughly C$50-150M; option economics of C$0.1-1M cash/shares plus C$3-15M of optionee-funded spend (the spend goes into the ground, not to the vendor); survey-stage block value of about C$0.3-1.5M once ranked. The WebSearch budget (200/turn, shared) was exhausted before this refuter ran, and one WebFetch (Wikipedia EMX) returned 404. Market-cap and royalty-revenue figures for EMX, Skyharbour and CanAlaska could not be re-sourced and are marked as estimates. Sources: https://www.skyharbourltd.com/projects/prospect-generator ; https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/2026/03/world-exploration-trends-2026-what-the-latest-data-says-about-budgets-risk-appetite-and-the-project-pipeline
votes.what_would_save_it: The idea survives only if the company stops being a junior-funded prospect generator and sells to or partners with buyers who are not cyclical. Three things would do it. (1) Majors or strategics (Cameco, Orano, Kazatomprom, utilities, sovereign funds) commit to buying ranked-corridor packages or a pre-agreed pipeline at much higher step-ups, or co-fund in exchange for first rights. (2) The archive pipeline proves a large hit-rate lift (2-3x more drill-worthy conductors per lapsed claim, shown on a blind backtest) that conventional re-inversion cannot match, making ML the enabling factor. (3) The model scales across many jurisdictions and commodities (Cu, Ni, REE, Au via BC ARIS, Ontario, Quebec, Australia's open-file data), so the NSR book is large enough to be a portfolio, not a lottery ticket. Even then it most plausibly becomes a mid-cap royalty company, not a venture-scale outcome. It would also have to be clearly separated from Terranox's own SMAD-to-rights loop.

votes.strongest_objection: The physics does not support the claim that re-processing yields drill-ready ground. Re-inverting or ML-merging legacy airborne EM cannot add information the original system never recorded. What limits the data is the system's bandwidth, transmitter moment, line spacing and navigation accuracy, not the processing. In the Athabasca, a helicopter TDEM conductor is a necessary input but a weak one. Most basement EM conductors are barren graphitic pelites. The things that separate a uranium target from barren graphite are the alteration halo (clay, desilicification, resistivity lows in the sandstone), structural offsets and geochemistry, and none of these resolves in airborne EM. Seeing them takes ground DC resistivity, ground or fixed-loop TEM, MT, or drilling. So the 'ranked conductor corridor' state this company would sell is low-information, and it is the same state the previous holder had just before walking away (adverse selection). The re-inversion step is the commodity part (Maxwell or plate modelling), and the ML lever sits on that part, not on the step that actually separates hits from misses. The pre-1990 INPUT archive (about 1,118 scanned surveys) is worse still. It is low-moment and narrow-band, positioned before GPS with errors of roughly 50-150 m (estimate), and survives only as profile maps or anomaly picks. Digitised, it yields conductor picks, not data you can invert, and those picks were long ago compiled into the provincial and company conductor databases. The headline cost figure (US$50-80M to replace the archive) is a cost-to-replace number, not a value. Much of the post-2000 HTEM ground has already been followed up with ground EM or drilling, which the public assessment files would show.
votes.evidence:
**The searches could not be run.** The shared WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was already used up when this verifier started, and all 3 searches were refused. Of the WebFetch attempts, the Greenridge press release returned HTTP 503 (unverified again), CanLII (the Saskatchewan Mineral Tenure Registry Regulations) returned HTTP 403, and the Saskatchewan TMEI FAQ PDF did parse. What follows is that one sourced finding plus domain reasoning, with each unsourced figure marked as an estimate. A follow-up message can resume searching.

**Findings**

1. **Sourced, from the TMEI 2026-27 FAQ (publications.saskatchewan.ca/.../91967).** The province's Targeted Mineral Exploration Incentive pays a 25% grant only for drilling, borehole geophysics and ground geophysics. The FAQ text says "The 2026-27 TMEI has expanded again to include borehole geophysical surveys and ground geophysical surveys", and work must relate to "drilling, borehole geophysical surveying, or ground geophysical surveying." It names no airborne work and no reprocessing.
   - The policy signal is that the province treats ground and drill follow-up as the step that adds information. Desk reprocessing gets no grant.
   - Whether reprocessing earns assessment credit is still unverified. Saskatchewan claim work requirements of roughly C$15-25/ha/yr (estimate) mean that a land bank of 100,000 ha would need about C$1.5-2.5M/yr of creditable work, or the claims lapse. That breaks the "staking cost only" premise, because C1's "trivial physical step" becomes a recurring cash cost.

2. **Depth physics (estimate).** Depth to the Athabasca unconformity runs from about 0 m at the rim to more than 1,000 m in the centre. Helicopter TDEM such as VTEM has an effective depth of investigation of about 300-500 m in resistive sandstone, depending on the conductor (estimate).
   - Inside the basin, deep conductors are poorly resolved or missed. That is why operators run ground fixed-loop or moving-loop TEM and DC resistivity before drilling.
   - At the shallow margins, where airborne EM works best, ground has been staked, flown and drilled many times over 50 years.
   - The niche where airborne-only data is decisive is therefore small.

3. **Information limit of re-inversion (physics).** Re-inversion refines plate depth, dip and conductance. It cannot recover channels that were never recorded, lines that were never flown (legacy spacing of about 200-400 m, estimate), or the system waveform and calibration that older digital filings often lack (estimate).
   - ML levelling across VTEM, AeroTEM and HeliTEM data is cosmetic for targeting. Merged amplitude grids do not change which discrete conductors exist.
   - The "1.5-3x hit-rate lever" applies to a step (conductor geometry) that is not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is fertile versus barren graphite.

4. **Adverse selection (logic plus the public record).** The same public assessment files that release the data also show any ground EM or drilling done before the lapse. Corridors that lapse with no follow-up were often judged barren after cheap ground checks, or were too deep to matter (estimate).

5. **Greenridge proof case.** It is still unverified (503). As described in the pitch, it used standard parametric plate re-inversion, not ML. "15 km of untested strike" is a conductor-length claim, not a hit-rate claim. Typical Athabasca conductor-to-deposit ratios are very low: hundreds to thousands of km of conductor per deposit (estimate).

6. **Cost claims.** The US$125-200/lkm and US$50-80M "replacement value" figures carry over from the pitch without a source. Even if they are right, they measure what it cost to collect the data, not what the data is worth. Legacy coverage over ground that has since been drilled is worth close to nothing.

**Verdict:** refuted. The physical and information step that decides value (ground follow-up, alteration mapping, drilling) is not abstracted away, so C1 fails on physics. ML is not what makes the work solvable, so C3 fails. Holding costs undercut "staking cost only."

**Sources**
- https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/91967/formats/108905/download (TMEI 2026-27 FAQ, fetched and parsed)
- https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/greenridge-exploration-identifies-uranium-targets-airborne-electromagnetic-survey (HTTP 503, unverified)
- https://www.canlii.org/en/sk/laws/regu/rrs-c-c-50.2-reg-31/latest/rrs-c-c-50.2-reg-31.html (HTTP 403, Section 68 unverified)
votes.what_would_save_it:
Four things would have to be shown with sources:
1. The public Section 68 releases include full multi-channel located data with system waveforms, so they can be properly re-inverted, rather than only grids or plate picks.
2. A measurable set of lapsed Athabasca claims, with conductors at depths where airborne data is enough to decide, that had no ground EM or drill follow-up before the lapse.
3. Saskatchewan gives assessment credit for reprocessing or reinterpreting existing data, so the ground can be held at desk cost.
4. Most important: a demonstrated way to use legacy airborne data, together with public SMAD geochemistry and drill logs, to tell fertile conductors from barren graphitic ones. That would move the lever onto the step that actually decides value.

Without point 4 it stays a commodity re-inversion service bolted onto a prospect generator. That is close to a Terranox data-layer feature, not a new company.

votes.strongest_objection:
Lapse Capital is not a new company. It is the existing Athabasca prospect-generator model, which Skyharbour, CanAlaska, Eagle Plains, Forum, F3 and Stallion already run: re-work legacy data, stake cheap ground, vend it for cash, shares and NSRs. Terranox's own loop (public Saskatchewan records, then ML, then cheap rights) already covers it, with geophysics files simply added to the data feed.

The defensibility is near zero. Claim lapses are public on MARS in real time, so the staking race is won in hours by whoever watches the feed. Section 68 releases the same raw data to every competitor at the same moment. Re-inverting VTEM is commodity work that CGI, Mira and Condor do with conventional codes. And the majors (Cameco, Denison, Orano) already hold the processed versions of the most valuable legacy Athabasca EM.

Adverse selection makes the lapsed corridors systematically worse: ground lapses because its owner, holding better data, chose not to drill it. On top of that, ML is not what makes the work solvable; the Greenridge proof case used standard parametric re-inversion. So the idea fails the founder's "ML must be the enabler" test and the venture-ceiling test. Vending income is about US$5-30M/yr (estimate), and generator peers are worth roughly US$0.05-0.5B (estimate).

votes.what_would_save_it:
To survive, the idea would need four things to hold together:

1) **A proprietary data edge, not just a speed edge.** Examples: digitising the roughly 1,118 scanned pre-1990 INPUT surveys, which only vision models make cheap and which no generator has done; or licensing or buying the majors' private processed inversions.

2) **Inverted adverse selection.** It would need evidence that lapsed ground holds systematically under-tested conductors. One example is surveys whose owner died or went bankrupt during the 2011-2020 uranium bust, rather than ground dropped after drilling.

3) **ML that is enabling, not incremental.** A benchmark would have to show that ML levelling and cross-system merging produces conductor picks that a CGI or Mira re-inversion cannot, at 10-100x lower cost per survey. That would let the pipeline cover the entire multi-province archive the day files release, at a scale no manual consultancy can match.

4) **A ceiling outside vending.** The model should be explicitly a royalty or streaming vehicle that holds NSRs across thousands of claims in five or more jurisdictions, financed like a royalty company.

Even then, it remains structurally a Terranox data-layer extension. It works best as a Terranox feature or a spin-out, not as an independent venture.

name: Lapsed-Survey Refinery and Land Bank (data that becomes public when claims lapse, turned into ground the company owns)

votes.strongest_objection: The money runs out and the buyers are the wrong kind. Every company that already runs this exact model (stake or reprocess ground, then option it to partners for earn-ins plus an NSR) is either loss-making with no revenue or a sub-US$30M/yr royalty business that took 20 years to build. CanAlaska is the Athabasca generator that flies and reprocesses VTEM. It is worth C$67M, with no revenue and a net loss of C$17.7M TTM. Skyharbour, the partner-funded-earn-in generator, is worth C$82M with no revenue. EMX Royalty is the best global example of the generator-to-royalty path. After about 20 years it had only US$27.5M revenue (2024), then gave up its independence by merging into Elemental Altus (EMX delisted Nov 2025, at about US$444M market cap). Altius is the only multi-billion name (C$3.3B, C$77M TTM revenue), and its value came from buying cash-flowing royalties (Voisey's Bay, potash, LIORC iron ore) with balance-sheet capital (domain knowledge, not fetched). Project generation was never the main driver. The people who pay for 'ranked-conductor / drill-ready' ground are cash-constrained juniors, who pay in stock and staged earn-ins inside a pro-cyclical market. Budgets fell for a third year to US$12.4B in 2025, and grassroots work hit a record-low share (S&P, from the brief; I could not re-fetch it, 403). The step-up at this rung is about 3-10x (estimate), not 10^4. The proposal's own ceiling estimate is US$10-40M/yr per jurisdiction, which is a tool-market-sized business rather than venture scale. The scarce input is open ground over good surveys, and that ground is adversely selected: holders drop it after flying it and finding nothing. Compute is not the scarce input, so ML is not what makes this solvable. It also sits almost on top of Terranox's own model (public Saskatchewan data, stake, prove), so the likeliest outcome is a Terranox module, not a separate company.

Quotes for CanAlaska, Skyharbour and Altius are as of 16 Oct 2026, from stockanalysis.com.

- **EMX:** revenue went US$5.65M (2020), 7.53M, 18.28M, 26.62M, US$27.45M (2024). It was delisted on 13 Nov 2025 after merging into Elemental Altus (ELEMF).
- **Pattern:** the pure generators that use this exact model are not profitable and are capped at C$60-100M. The one ladder that worked (EMX) peaked at about US$27M/yr revenue after about two decades, then consolidated.

**Market-ceiling arithmetic (all estimates)**
- About 335 post-2000 helicopter EM surveys in Saskatchewan, many over ground still held. Suppose 10-30 parcels a year come off confidentiality and are still open and worth staking. If each is optioned at C$0.3-1.5M of cash and stock spread over 3-5 years, that is about C$5-20M/yr gross per jurisdiction.
- Most of that is paid in illiquid junior shares. NSRs on grassroots ground have well under a 5% chance of reaching production (estimate), and only after 10-15 years.
- Five or more jurisdictions gives roughly US$25-100M/yr at peak cycle, and it falls sharply in down-cycles. Funding the land bank needs balance-sheet capital, which a VC fund would be backing as an exploration fund.

**Who pays**
- **Juniors:** cash-poor and cyclical. They pay in shares and earn-in work commitments, not cash.
- **Majors:** buy at the resource or discovery stage, not the conductor-ranked stage.
- **Data buyers:** a library sale is a small market. Xcalibur/Getech-type 'Earth intelligence' players sit at tens of millions in revenue (Getech is an AIM small-cap; brief, not re-fetched).

**Not verified this pass**
- The Saskatchewan s.68 confidentiality terms. The document I fetched was the TMEI PDF, not the regulation.
- The S&P figure of US$12.4B for 2025 (the page returned 403).
votes.what_would_save_it:
The idea survives only if it stops being a project generator. Three things would each be needed.

1. **Capture value at a rung with a real step-up.** For example, use the refinery as the targeting engine for a balance-sheet discovery company that funds its own first drill holes on the best 1-2% of conductors. The value then comes from the 10^3-10^4 drill-hit step-up rather than the 3-10x survey-stage step-up. That makes it Terranox for all commodities and all jurisdictions, which brings in the cannibalisation problem.

2. **Find a large cash buyer for the derived layer.** This would mean showing that majors or sovereign surveys (GSC/NRCan, Geoscience Australia, Saudi Ma'aden-type programmes) pay US$1M+ per jurisdiction per year for levelled, re-inverted, analog-digitised national EM/mag compilations. It would also need proof that this is a US$500M+/yr market, which nothing gathered here supports.

3. **Prove that ML turns adversely-selected lapsed data into hits.** That needs a back-test on SMAD drill outcomes showing that ML re-inversion of dropped surveys finds conductors previous holders missed, at a rate of 1.5-3x or better. Without that, the input is ground the previous holders already flew and rejected.

Also open:
- Re-verify the s.68 release triggers.
- Count how many lapsed-survey parcels are actually open each year. If it is under about 50/yr across Canada plus Australia, the ceiling claim fails regardless.

votes.strongest_objection: Re-processing cannot add information that the original flight never measured. Each archived survey's depth of investigation is set by its physics: transmitter dipole moment, base frequency, line spacing and noise floor. Software or ML cannot raise that ceiling. Two facts bear on this. (a) The roughly 1,118 analog pre-1990 surveys (fixed-wing INPUT, a few channels, recorded on chart/film) and early-2000s helicopter systems are low-moment. One archived AeroTEM III survey states a 183 kNIA moment. (b) Deep Athabasca targets (unconformity 480-1,000 m; Cigar Lake at about 480 m, Cosa Ursa at 850-1,000 m) lie at or beyond the practical depth of investigation of even modern VTEM over conductive cover (estimate: about 300-500 m). The basin's deep exploration actually runs on ground moving-loop or SQUID TEM, DC resistivity and gravity. So the "virtual survey worth US$100k" on lapsed ground is mostly an already-extracted, depth-limited dataset. Reaching drill-ready still requires new physical acquisition (the brief's own NeoCore budget: C$200k ground EM + C$150k gravity), which is several times the airborne cost the idea claims to avoid. The physical step is not trivial, so C1 fails on physics, not just on market. Add adverse selection: lapsed ground is usually ground that the previous holder flew, interpreted and dropped. The thesis then reduces to "re-pick conductors the last geophysicist already rejected, on data too shallow to see the target".
votes.evidence:
Findings, with a caveat on method. The shared WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was already used up when I started, so every search returned 'not performed'. I could use only direct WebFetch of URLs carried from the brief. Whatever I could not verify is marked (estimate).

1. **Survey cost is about C$100k per ~750 line-km. This is real but small next to the downstream physical steps.** BC ARIS Report 32307 (Berg project, 2010, Terrane Metals) covers a helicopter AeroTEM III EM + mag survey of 754.35 line-km at 100 m spacing. Total cost was C$99,894, about C$132/line-km including support. The founder's ~US$100k figure checks out, and so does the idea's median of ~760 line-km. But at 100-200 m spacing, 760 line-km covers only about 76-150 km² (7,600-15,000 ha). The flight saved works out to about C$7-13/ha (estimate). That is much less than the drill-ready confirmation step: C$350k of ground EM + gravity per the brief's NeoCore figure, which I did not re-fetch.

2. **Physics limits are fixed in the archive.** The same report gives the AeroTEM III transmitter moment as 183 kNIA. In its system-comparison appendix the report notes that frequency-domain helicopter EM reaches 'excellent depth penetration (up to 100 m)', and that fixed-wing systems' 'only advantage' is depth penetration. So older or low-moment data has a hard depth ceiling. Athabasca unconformity targets sit at 480-1,000 m (brief). Inverting processed, decimated or analog data (chart profiles with ~6 INPUT channels) cannot recover late-time response that was never recorded. Re-inversion also needs the exact system waveform, calibration, bird altitude and raw or minimally filtered channels. Many archived filings hold only grids, PDF maps and anomaly picks (estimate), which rules out 'complete digital listings'-grade inversion for much of the 1,831 records.

3. **Cross-system 'levelling and merging' is not physically valid for EM.** INPUT, AeroTEM, VTEM, HeliTEM and ZTEM have different footprints, waveforms, time gates and (for ZTEM) a different physical quantity: natural-field tipper, not controlled-source TEM. Their responses to the same conductor are not related by a calibration offset. Magnetics and radiometrics can be levelled and merged, as the GSC routinely does. EM can only be merged at the interpretation level (conductor axes), which reduces the 'refinery' to compiling conductor picks. Generators and the provincial survey already do that.

4. **The Greenridge 2014 '15+ km of conductors' example is weak support.** I could not fetch the source (HTTP 503). As described, it is a re-inversion of the company's own recent VTEM survey, not lapsed third-party data, and 'mostly untested conductors' is not a hit-rate result. Athabasca graphitic conductors are abundant and overwhelmingly barren. The conductor is a pathfinder, not the target, so better conductor geometry moves the hit rate little. Alteration, structure, gravity lows and resistivity lows, mostly from ground or deeper methods, carry the discriminating signal (estimate).

5. **The learned or amortised inversion lever addresses a cost that is not the bottleneck.** Parametric plate inversion (Maxwell-style) of one ~760 line-km survey takes a geophysicist days and costs C$5-20k (estimate). Supervision for 'ranking conductors against SMAD drill outcomes' is sparse: a few dozen Athabasca deposits (estimate) and drill holes biased toward already-favoured conductors. So the 1.5-3x hit-rate claim has no physical or statistical support.

6. **CanAlaska flies its own surveys rather than reusing lapsed data.** It is flying about 2,481 line-km of new VTEM Plus at 200 m spacing plus 8,861 line-km of mag/radiometrics at 50 m near Key Lake, describing the area as having 'very limited exploration work'. Even the leading Athabasca generator, holding about 500,000 ha, buys new modern data instead of relying on legacy surveys. That is consistent with legacy data being too low in quality or depth to substitute.

7. **I could not verify the confidentiality regime.** The Saskatchewan PDF in the brief (publications.saskatchewan.ca 91967) turned out to be the Targeted Mineral Exploration Incentive FAQ, not the Mineral Tenure Registry Regulations. CanLII returned 403. The s.68 'earliest of 3 years / consent / lapse' release rule is still an unverified claim. The FAQ does show that the province demands 'Geospatial geophysical dataset and digital maps' from the contractor for incentive claims, and that the incentive program has funded only C$3.2M of geophysical work in total (2018-2026). That points to a small flow of newly filed digital geophysics (estimate: tens of surveys a year).

Net result: the cost claim (~US$100k per survey) is true. The substitution claim, that a lapsed archived survey equals a US$100k virtual survey that makes the physical step trivial, fails on depth-of-investigation physics, on missing raw data and system metadata in archives, and on the non-mergeability of EM across systems. The ML claim targets a non-bottleneck.

Sources:
- https://apps.nrs.gov.bc.ca/pub/aris/Report/32307.pdf/ (C$99,894 for 754.35 line-km AeroTEM III, 2010; 183 kNIA moment; HEM penetration ~100 m remark)
- https://www.juniorminingnetwork.com/junior-miner-news/press-releases/895-tsx-venture/cvv/160027-canalaska-starts-airborne-surveys-near-key-lake-mine-and-mill-in-southeastern-athabasca-basin.html (2,481 line-km VTEM Plus at 200 m; 8,861 line-km mag/rad; ~500,000 ha held)
- https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/91967/formats/108905/download (TMEI FAQ: C$3.2M geophysics funded 2018-26; contractor digital dataset requirement)
- https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/greenridge-exploration-identifies-uranium-targets-airborne-electromagnetic-survey (could not fetch, HTTP 503)
votes.what_would_save_it:
Narrow the thesis to the subset where the physics works and the data is complete, then prove that subset is large. The subset would be: post-2010 high-moment full-waveform helicopter TEM (VTEM Plus/Max, HeliTEM, 400+ kNIA), filed with raw channels, waveform and altitude, over targets shallower than ~300-400 m (eastern Athabasca rim, basement-hosted Patterson-corridor-style targets, plus non-uranium shallow VMS/Ni/graphite), on ground that is open or lapsed now. Needed evidence:
(1) A count, from the SK Airborne Surveys layer joined to current tenure, of such surveys over currently open ground (needs to be hundreds, not tens).
(2) Verified confidentiality and lapse release text and actual file completeness (raw .gdb/.xyz with waveform, not grids or PDFs).
(3) A back-test showing that re-inverting legacy surveys over ground later drilled would have ranked the eventual mineralised conductors in the top decile, at materially better than the original contractor's picks.
(4) Evidence that a buyer pays for 'ranked conductor' ground without new ground geophysics.
Without (3) and (4), the physical step (ground EM/gravity, ~C$350k) stays the gate, and the idea is a cheaper-desktop-study feature, most naturally a Terranox module.

votes.strongest_objection:
The defensible core of this idea is a cheap derivative layer over public files, and incumbents already sit on it. The other half, staking ground that has been surveyed but not drilled, is what Athabasca project generators already do as their whole business. They don't need ML to do it.

Generators like CanAlaska, Skyharbour and Eagle Plains, and the earlier Kenorland/Fortune Bay/Purepoint group, already read the same Saskatchewan assessment filings, re-process them with one in-house geophysicist or a CGI/Mira contract, stake the open ground and option it out. On the data side, Xcalibur (multi-client libraries plus the PGW interpretation unit, EMerald and a 25.5% Getech stake) and Terranox itself are a short step from the same claim-indexed conductor model.

Nothing here is proprietary. The raw files are public by law, open to anyone, and become free once confidentiality ends, so any competitor (Terranox included) can rebuild the refinery. Generic geophysics ML tools copy the ML layer quickly.

The one scarce input is open ground over good conductors, and that ground suffers adverse selection: holders usually drop claims after their own survey and interpretation found nothing.

The CanAlaska Key Lake release (100%-owned ground) shows generators fly new, tighter VTEM Plus anyway (about 2,481 line-km at 200 m spacing, plus about 8,861 line-km of mag/radiometrics at 50 m) to get a single levelled dataset, with no mention of reusing historic data. That undercuts the claim that legacy surveys substitute for the roughly US$100k flight.

There is also direct overlap: the same public Saskatchewan data, then stake, then prove is Terranox's own loop. That makes it a Terranox module that is trivially absorbed, not a separate company.

**Carried from the brief (unverified):**
- Xcalibur bought PGW's interpretation unit and EMerald Geomodelling and holds 25.5% of Getech, i.e. it is moving toward an "Earth Intelligence" layer over its libraries (https://tunnellingjournal.com/xcalibur-acquires-emerald-geomodelling-to-strengthen-subsurface-modelling/, https://www.ajbell.co.uk/news/articles/getch-highlights-growing-order-book-loss-narrows-higher-revenue).

- S&P: global nonferrous exploration budgets fell for a third year to about US$12.4B in 2025, and grassroots work hit a record-low share, so buyers of survey-stage ground are shrinking (https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/2026/03/world-exploration-trends-2026-what-the-latest-data-says-about-budgets-risk-appetite-and-the-project-pipeline).

**Defensibility analysis:**
1. *Data moat = 0.* The inputs are statutory public filings (Saskatchewan SMAD/Airborne Surveys layer, Ontario OGS, BC ARIS, Manitoba, Quebec, WA WAMEX). Anyone can download them once confidentiality ends.
2. *Processing moat = low.* Levelling, plate inversion and anomaly picking are mature commercial tools (Geosoft/Seequent Oasis montaj, Maxwell, EMIT, CGI/Mira services). Learned or amortised inversions are active academic work and would spread within 1-2 years (estimate). Vision/OCR on scanned maps is commodity.
3. *Land moat = adverse selection.* Every competing generator, and Terranox, also watches claim lapses. In the Athabasca, open ground over credible conductors is picked over, and lapses mostly follow negative interpretation (estimate).
4. *Buyer step-up is small.* By the idea's own figures it is about 3-10x from raw ground to drill-ready, not 10^4. The buyers are cash-constrained juniors in a down-cycle market.
5. *Physics limit.* The roughly 1,118 analog pre-1990 INPUT surveys are low-moment and shallow, so they cannot see 480-1,000 m unconformity targets. The fresh 200 m VTEM Plus at CanAlaska is evidence that the industry treats legacy coverage as insufficient.
6. *Cannibalisation.* It is the same data, frame and loop as Terranox, so Terranox absorbs it as a feature.

Score as given: 14/25. ML is not what makes it solvable.

name: Speculative Fly-First, Stake-First Multi-Client Surveys (privatising the QUEST effect)

votes.strongest_objection: The money that pays for this is small. Worldwide, airborne surveys for mineral exploration are a few-hundred-million-dollar market (estimate, US$400-700M/yr), and governments give the same kind of data away free to attract exploration investment: Geoscience BC QUEST, NRCan GEM, the Saskatchewan Geological Survey, USGS Earth MRI and Geoscience Australia AusAEM. That leaves a private multi-client library with no pricing power. The TGS analogy fails because TGS sells repeatedly to dozens of oil majors, each with a US$100M-plus exploration budget, and each seismic dataset feeds a hydrocarbon licensing round. A mineral EM block has about 3-10 buyers, mostly juniors raising C$1-5M at a time, who pay mostly in shares and work commitments. Viridien/CGG kept its mineral multi-client library when it sold the airborne unit to Xcalibur in 2021, and that library never became a material revenue line. That is direct evidence that the mineral multi-client pool is small. The value capture therefore falls back to prospect generation (stake and vend). Listed prospect generators such as EMX, Altius, Eagle Plains, CanAlaska and Kenorland earn US$10-50M/yr from optioning and royalties after decades of work. Only a royalty tail that hits a mine reaches US$100M+/yr, so this is a slow royalty company, not a venture-scale data company. On who pays: the pre-sold pooled slots that fund 30-50% of the campaign are a one-off contractor-margin service. Survey contractors (Geotech, Xcalibur, Axiom, Expert Geophysics) already sell these and capture that margin, and buying flights from them keeps the founder's margin thin. Finally, ML does not unlock this business. Its binding constraints are capital (about US$1-1.5M per block), free-riding (competitors stake around any visible staking rush) and buyer count, not prediction. In Saskatchewan uranium it is literally Terranox's next step.
votes.evidence:
Research limits: both WebSearch calls I made were refused because the shared 200-search budget for this turn was used up. The evidence below comes from the supplied brief plus prior knowledge, and figures not re-verified are marked.

1) Multi-client economics. The TGS FY2025 figures (US$883.8M multi-client sales on US$446.8M investment, from the brief, not re-verified) are almost entirely oil and gas seismic sold to dozens of capitalised majors. The mineral multi-client pool is small by comparison:
- Viridien/CGG kept its multi-physics multi-client library at the 2021 sale of the airborne unit to Xcalibur, and the library has not been a material reported line since (estimate, from knowledge).
- Mineral blocks have about 3-10 buyers each (brief).

2) Free government substitutes. QUEST spent about C$5M of public money and gave the data away, and that free release is what triggered roughly 200,000 ha of staking (brief, unverified). A private operator that withholds the data loses the "public-release rush" mechanism that created the value in the first place. There is ongoing free regional EM from NRCan GEM, Saskatchewan, Ontario, USGS Earth MRI and AusAEM, so any private licence price is capped near zero for regional-scale data.

3) Who pays and how:
- Juniors option ground mostly with work commitments and shares, about C$0.3-5M per block (brief, estimate), not with cash.
- Grassroots exploration's share of budgets was at a record low in 2025 (S&P World Exploration Trends 2026, from the brief), so the buyer pool is shrinking and pro-cyclical.
- Majors (Cameco, Orano) generate their own targets and fly their own surveys.

4) Ceiling comparables:
- Prospect-generator and royalty companies (EMX, Altius) took 15-25 years to reach about US$0.3-1.5B market cap (estimate), mostly through royalties on mines found by others.
- Pure generators (Eagle Plains, CanAlaska) are sub-US$100M market cap (estimate).

5) Capital intensity: a 10,000 line-km VTEM campaign cost about US$1.4M (Loncor/Randgold, from the brief). That is per-block capex at risk every season, versus about US$1/ha staking, so the physical step is not trivial.

6) Overlap with Terranox: an ML target, then fly, then stake sequence on Saskatchewan uranium is Terranox's own pipeline step.
votes.what_would_save_it:
Moving off the data-licensing model entirely, so the business becomes an ML-placed, survey-backed land and royalty company outside Saskatchewan uranium. Examples would be deep-cover copper or nickel in Canada, the US or Australia under the US critical-minerals push. It would only rescue the ceiling if it could show three things:
- **Better placement:** ML-placed speculative blocks give at least a 2x higher option or royalty conversion rate than government-free regional data plus a normal generator, backtested on SMAD/CAGDB or ARIS outcomes.
- **Real buyers:** majors (not juniors) sign pre-commitments, for example strategic-alliance funding of US$5-20M/yr such as BHP Xplor or Rio Tinto generative alliances.
- **Value captured:** retained royalties of 1-3% NSR across 50+ optioned blocks, so that one or two mine discoveries produce a royalty stream worth US$100M+/yr.

Alternatively, a step-change in cost (autonomous drone EM at under US$30/line-km, sustained) could make the "physical step is trivial" claim true. That would let the company fly continent-scale ground speculatively, with the information step dominating. Without major-funded alliances or a royalty-heavy structure, the realistic ceiling stays at about US$15-80M/yr (estimate).

votes.strongest_objection: The QUEST analogy does not hold up on cost per km², and that breaks the unit economics. QUEST's value came from very cheap, coarse regional data: about C$5M over about 46,000 km², roughly C$110/km². Its airborne gravity and VTEM were flown at multi-km line spacing (spacing recalled from memory, not re-verified). The proposed private product is 100-200 m-spaced EM: 10,000 line-km for about US$1.4M over 1,000-2,000 km². That is about US$700-1,400/km², or C$1,000-1,900/km², which is 10-17x QUEST's cost density. At 400 m spacing, as in the one sourced comparable (Loncor/Randgold), 10,000 km covers about 4,000 km². So the company is not 'privatising QUEST'. It is buying ground-truth-grade data at 10x+ the cost per km² that produced the QUEST staking rush, and selling it to 3-10 buyers per block. The physics compounds this in Saskatchewan uranium. The airborne EM target is the graphitic basement conductor, not the uranium. Uranium is non-conductive, and most Athabasca conductors are barren graphitic pelites (well-known exploration fact; no sourced hit-rate number). The step-up for 'ground with a conductor' is therefore only about 10^1-10^2, nowhere near Terranox's 10^4. Two zones remain. In the shallow eastern basin and basin-margin zones, where airborne EM resolves basement conductors well, the ground has already been flown repeatedly (INPUT in the 1970s, then GEOTEM, MEGATEM and VTEM) and heavily staked. In the deep western and central basin, where ground is still open, conductors sit under roughly 500-1,000 m of sandstone, at or beyond practical helicopter TDEM depth of investigation (estimate). That is why the industry there uses ground MLTEM/SWML and DC resistivity. The 'open ground + no modern EM + airborne-resolvable' intersection that the value-of-information model needs is small. The physical step is also a US$1-1.5M seasonal capex bet, about 1,000x the staking cost. It is not trivial, so C1 fails on the founder's own definition.
votes.evidence:
Sourced:
(1) Loncor/Randgold Ngayu VTEM, 2016: 10,000 line-km total for about US$1.4M (about US$140/line-km all-in), at 400 m spacing tightened to 200 m over targets, over a 2,077 km² permit area (https://geotech.ca/loncor-shares-higher-following-news-that-randgold-to-start-vtem-geophysical-survey-over-loncors-ngayu-project-stock-up-nearly-5/). Line-spacing arithmetic: 10,000 km at 400 m is about 4,000 km²; at 200 m about 2,000 km²; at 100 m about 1,000 km². The pitch's 1,000-2,000 km² footprint therefore implies 100-200 m spacing, i.e. about US$700-1,400/km².
(2) Cameco holds 660,000 ha directly in northern Saskatchewan, 'including many of the most prospective areas of the Athabasca Basin'. It spent more than C$12M on regional exploration in 2025 and plans about C$14M for regional Saskatchewan in 2026, combining 'target generation geophysical surveys with diamond drilling' (https://www.cameco.com/businesses/uranium-projects/exploration). The largest capitalised buyer already generates its own airborne targets on the best ground, so it is a competitor, not a customer.
(3) QUEST: about C$5M over 46,000 km², from the brief. My Geoscience BC fetch returned 404, so this is not re-verified. On those figures QUEST cost about C$110/km², versus about C$1,000-1,900/km² for the proposed product.

Unsourced, from prior knowledge, marked (estimate):
- Athabasca airborne EM coverage is dense in the eastern basin from decades of INPUT/GEOTEM/MEGATEM/VTEM flying (estimate).
- Basement conductors in the deep central and western basin sit at roughly 500-1,000 m depth, where ground EM is standard (estimate).
- Most conductors are graphitic and barren (estimate; no hit-rate number sourced).
- Saskatchewan claim maintenance is about C$15/ha/yr from year 2 (estimate). Filed assessment reports become public after a confidentiality period, which ends the data moat on staked ground (estimate).
- The 1.5x airborne assessment credit is unverified.
- TGS's 2.0x sales-to-investment ratio rests on dozens of oil majors buying seismic. Mineral blocks have 3-10 junior buyers, and governments (NRCan, SGS, USGS Earth MRI, AusAEM) release comparable regional EM free (estimate).

Research limits: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was used up before I could search. Direct fetches of the Geoscience BC and Saskatchewan regulation pages returned 404. Only the Geotech and Cameco pages were verified.
votes.what_would_save_it:
1) Move out of Saskatchewan uranium, to avoid Terranox overlap and dense legacy coverage, into a commodity whose target responds directly to airborne EM, where a conductor-hit step-up is closer to 10^3: massive Ni-Cu-PGE or VMS sulphides in under-flown Canadian Shield, Nunavut or Ontario cover, where the conductor often is the ore.
2) Fly QUEST-density regional data (1-4 km spacing, about C$100-300/km²). Spend the capex only to find where to infill, and charge for 100-200 m infill only after pooled pre-sales.
3) Validate the ML value-of-information lift on a backtest: hold out historical surveys from SMAD/MNDM archives and show that the model ranks the blocks that later produced stakeable conductors and drill discoveries 2-3x better than random or expert selection.
4) Pre-sell 50%+ of each campaign to pooled claim-holders, verifying the assessment credit multiplier, so speculative capex per season is below about US$0.5M.
5) Take royalties rather than one-off option payments, so the ceiling runs through an EMX/Altius-style tail. That tail exists, but it is slow, and it still is not ML-gated.
Even with all five, the binding constraints (buyer count, free government data, disclosure expiry, pro-cyclical junior financing) are not prediction problems. So ML stays a nice-to-have, and the idea most likely stays below venture scale.

votes.strongest_objection:
This is not a new company category. It is the prospect-generator model (generate targets with your own regional geophysics, stake, vend for cash, shares and royalties) with a multi-client data library added. Both halves are already occupied, and neither half has a moat.

(1) Prospect generators already do fly-first, stake-first:
- Kenorland's model is "systematic, property-wide, phased exploration surveys" funded by option-to-JV partners. It has 19 projects (13 owned, 5 optioned, 1 royalty), a 4% NSR on Sumitomo's Frotet discovery, and Franco-Nevada became a significant shareholder in October 2026.
- In the Athabasca, CanAlaska, Skyharbour, Eagle Plains, Purepoint and Fortune Bay all run generate, stake, vend. EMX and Altius run the royalty version.
- None of these is a venture-scale outcome. The best are worth roughly US$0.3-1.5B (estimate) after 10-20 years.

(2) The multi-client mineral airborne library has been tried and was deprioritised. CGG/Viridien sold its airborne unit to Xcalibur in 2021. The reason is structural: free government data (Geoscience BC, NRCan GEM, provincial surveys, USGS Earth MRI, AusAEM) caps prices, and each block has only about 3-10 buyers, against dozens of oil majors per seismic basin. The TGS 2.0x sales-to-investment ratio does not transfer.

(3) Nothing in the stack is defensible:
- Flying is a commodity bought per line-km from Geotech, Axiom, Xcalibur, SkyTEM or Expert Geophysics, and anyone with about US$1.4M can buy the same 10,000 line-km.
- Pooled "block survey" slots to share mobilisation are already standard contractor practice.
- The ML placement model is a copyable layer. KoBold (US$1B+ raised, owns ground), Earth AI (targets, stakes and drills itself), Fleet Space (cheap ambient-noise seismic acquisition) and Terranox itself already do AI-targeting-then-own-ground.
- The "proprietary" period is short. Staking is visible at once on Saskatchewan's MARS claim map, so competitors stake around any cluster of fresh claims. Assessment filings needed to hold claims become public after a confidentiality period (about 3 years, estimate), so the data moat on staked ground expires by design.

(4) In Saskatchewan uranium this is literally Terranox's next pipeline step (ML target, then fly, then stake). That violates the "not a Terranox feature" rule. Moving to other provinces or commodities only puts it in Kenorland and KoBold's territory.

(5) ML is not the binding constraint. Capital per block, free-riding on public staking, government data giveaways and a thin pro-cyclical junior buyer base are. The rubric itself says ml_is_what_makes_it_solvable = false. QUEST's 200,000 ha staking response came from free public release in a hot market, not from targeting.

votes.what_would_save_it:
Three changes, any one of which could move it toward a pass, but none is evidenced yet:

1. **Own a cheaper sensor.** The economics improve sharply if the company owns a sensor and acquisition method an order of magnitude cheaper than crewed helicopter TDEM. Examples are drone or fixed-wing autonomous EM, or passive or ambient-noise methods, at under US$20/line-km with no crewed mobilisation. Then flying speculatively over whole districts is trivial in the Terranox sense, and the data asset cannot be bought by competitors from Geotech.

2. **Validate the placement model.** Show with a retrospective backtest on SMAD and assessment archives that the value-of-information model at least doubles the share of conductors that later get drilled or optioned. That would make ML the real lever rather than garnish.

3. **Go where the public data does not exist.** Operate in jurisdictions with no free government EM, map-staking, and long confidentiality windows, outside Saskatchewan uranium to avoid Terranox overlap. Then monetise mainly through retained royalties and carried interests, the EMX, Altius and Kenorland route, rather than data licences, accepting a 10-20 year path to a US$1B+ outcome.

Even then, it competes head-on with Kenorland, KoBold and Earth AI, so differentiation would have to come from the proprietary low-cost sensor, not from the business model.
